sale_title: The Bennett & Judie Weinstock Collection: Part I
description_block:
A Prattware Model of a Performing Horse, Circa 1800
A lively ochre and brown spotted horse rearing up, its forelegs cycling above a gentleman lying on his back with arms raised, a stump supporting the animal's belly, the rectangular base painted with a trailing border, 7 1/2 in. (20.3cm) high

Provenance
Behar Collection

Literature
John and Griselda Lewis, Pratt Ware, 1984, p.277, fig.64.

This rare model appears to depict a circus act rather than an un-seated rider and defiant horse. The horse trainer is thought to represent Philip Astley, the 'father of modern circus', whose trick riding and showmanship earned him great renown in the late 18th and early 19th century in England and further afield. His 'Ampitheatre of the Arts' continued after his death in 1814 and is mentioned by authors ranging from Jane Austen to Charles Dickens. Astley as born in Newcastle-under-Lyme, Staffordshire, very close to the Potteries.

A very similar model was sold by Sotheby's on 26 October 2002, lot 1517. The same example is illustrated by Pat Halfpenny in English Earthenware Figures, 1991, dust jacket and p.121, fig.29 and appears again in Pat Halfpenny and Stella Beddoe's, Circus & Sport, 1990, cover image and p.15, no.7.

sale_title: The Bennett & Judie Weinstock Collection: Part I
description_block:
'The Death of Munrow': An Impressive Staffordshire Pearlware Table Base Group, Circa 1825-30
Attributed to the 'Sherratt' pot bank, modeled as a huge striped tiger his jaws clamped around the head of a British officer, whose lifeless body slumps over the edge of the table base, raised on six feet molded with swags, titled 'THE DEATH OF MUNROW', 10 1/2 in. (27.7cm) high, 12 1/2 in. (33cm) long

In July 1793, the Gentleman's Magazine printed 'An Extract of a Letter from a Gentleman to his Friend at Calcutta'. The letter detailed the extraordinary fate of a young Lieutenant Munro, who had been out stalking deer in Mysore the previous December. On that particular day the hunting party suddenly "heard a roar, like thunder, and saw an immense Royal tiger spring on the unfortunate Munro". The beast tore away into the jungle, dragging the officer by his head, reportedly "with as much ease as I could lift a kitten". Munro somehow managed to stumble back to the camp but died of his significant wounds twenty-four hours later.

The death of this "amiable and promising youth" shook the British public to its core and the gruesome tale subsequently became inextricably linked to the famous wooden automaton 'Tippoo's Tiger'. Made for Tipu Sultan, the ruler of Mysore from 1782 to 1799, the large model depicts a tiger mauling a European soldier. A handle not only causes the man's arm to lift up and down but an organ concealed in the belly of the beast plays noises intended to imitate his dying groans. Tipu Sultan's vehement resistance to British rule came to an end in 1799 when he was killed during the siege of Seringapatam. The automaton was discovered in the Palace and was shipped to London where it was put on display at the British East India Company's museum, eventually being transferred to the Victoria & Albert Museum, where it currently resides, accession no.2545(IS).

The public display of Tipu's Tiger was most likely the catalyst for the Staffordshire potters who were already developing a penchant for depicting exotic animals and scandalous scenes. An engraving by W Cooke formed the frontispiece of A Review of the Origin, Progress and Result of the Decisive War with the Late Tippoo Sultan in Mysore, published in 1800, and it seems likely that it was a version of this print that was adapted to become 'The Death of Munrow', the former providing the iconography.

Myrna Schkolne illustrates and discusses a similar Staffordshire 'Death of Munrow', see Holding The Past: The William Herbert and Nancy Hunt Collection, 2014, pp.65-67. Further models can be found in public collections including the Victoria & Albert Museum, accession no.C.1-2007, the Fitzwilliam Museum, C.967-1928, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, 2016.129. An example was sold by Sotheby's on 7 April 2004, lot 15. Another from the Hope McCormick Collection, illustrated by Millie Manheim, 1980, pl.36, was subsequently sold by Christie's on 21 June 2003, lot 16.

sale_title: The Bennett & Judie Weinstock Collection: Part I
description_block:
A Staffordshire Pearlware 'Ale Bench' Table Base Group, circa 1830
Attributed to the 'Sherratt' pot bank, modeled as an enraged wife battling her inebriated husband, he on his back against a broken table, his ale jug broken at his feet, their yellow chairs before bocage and a turreted building forming spill holders, the mottled table base embossed with foliate swags and titled 'ALE BENCH', 7 1/2 in. (20.5cm) high, 8 in. (21.5cm) wide

Provenance
Christie's London, 18 June 1984, lot 86

A companion model to the following lot in this sale, which shows a happy and 'respectable' family having tea and cake. By contrast, this 'Ale Bench' group shows the destructive nature of drink in a society where the temperance movement was gathering support. A similar group is illustrated and discussed by Myrna Schkolne, see Holding the Past, The William Herbert and Nancy Hunt Collection, 2014, p.57. Curiously, a separate version of this 'Ale Bench' group was also made, depicting a more measured and serene scene, with the same couple seated in the chairs either side of the table, both are drinking beer. Beer was certainly viewed as a more respectable beverage compared with gin, which was increasingly demonized as the downfall of working class families. All three models, which demonstrate three stages of the temperance movement are illustrated by Rosalie Wise Sharp, Ceramics, Ethics and Scandal, 2002, pp.106-107.

provenance: Christie's London, 18 June 1984, lot 86

As similar group was sold by Bonhams on 16 May 2006, lot 146. Compared with the 'Ale Bench' group, the sober, tea-drinking family are wearing finer clothes, indicating a slight difference in class between the two.

sale_title: The Bennett & Judie Weinstock Collection: Part I
description_block:
The Red Barn Murder: A Staffordshire Pearlware Figure Group, Circa 1828
Attributed to the 'Patriotic Group' pot bank, the red wooden barn with thatched roof, flanked by two leafy trees, the figures of Maria Marten and William Corder standing before the doorway, a recumbent cow and two hens nearby, titled on the base "THE RED BARN NEAR POLSTEAD - BURY ST. EDMUNDS", 7 in. (19cm) high, 7 1/2 in. (20.2cm) wide

The infamous and salacious Red Barn Murder is discussed in detail by Myrna Schkolne, People, Passions, Pastimes, and Pleasures, 2006, pp.46-53. In 1826, a tenant farmer named William Corder began a relationship with Maria Marten. Already mother to two illegitimate children, Maria's third child, fathered by William, was born in 1827 and died shortly afterwards. In May that year William arranged to meet Maria at the barn on his family farm near Polstead so that they could travel together to Ipswich to marry. However, Maria's family never saw her again and after a suspicious series of events her father searching the Red Barn at his wife's request found her murdered body buried beneath the floor.

In August 1828, William Corder was convicted of Maria's murder and it was reported that some 10,000 people travelled to watch him hang. The public was equally outraged and fascinated by the crime and visitors flocked to the Red Barn, tearing the building apart and taking pieces as morbid souvenirs. 

Such huge popular interest moved the Staffordshire potters to produce a number of models of the Red Barn and of the protagonists of the tale. See the Sherratt-style table base models sold by Bonhams on 14 April 2010, lot 66. A version without the figures of Corden and Marten from the Hope McCormick Collection was sold by Christie's New York on 21 January 2003, lot 44. Another variation of the model from the Hunt Collection is illustrated by Myrna Schkolne, Holding the Past, 2014, pp.68-70.

A Pair of Staffordshire Pearlware Busts of King William IV and Queen Adelaide, Circa 1830-35
Attributed to the 'Sherratt' pot bank, the Royal pair in brightly enameled costume, the waisted socles titled 'KING WILLIAM THE FOURTH' and 'QUEEN ADAERLENE', raised on footed table bases molded with swags, 10 in. (25.4cm) high

In July 1818, a week after their first meeting, Prince William, Duke of Clarence married Princess Adelaide of Saxe-Meiningen who was 27 years his junior. Conceived as a marriage of convenience and necessity after the sudden death of Princess Charlotte, by all accounts the union appeared remarkably harmonious. When William acceded to the throne in 1830, Adelaide became Queen Consort until the King's death in 1837 when the crown passed to the young Princess Victoria. 

A similar pair of busts have different coloring on the table bases but the same unorthodox spelling of the Queen's name, see Myrna Schkolne, Obsession: The Myrna & Benzion Schkolne Collection of Early English Pottery, Vol.1, 2026, pp.102-4.

sale_title: The Bennett & Judie Weinstock Collection: Part I
description_block:
A Rare Staffordshire Pearlware Dovecote, Circa 1825
Possibly 'Sherratt' pot bank, the house-like structure raised on four paw and ball feet, five tiers with ledges accommodating sixteen openings, a bevy of doves perched within and on the exterior ledges, some seated on nests, or beside clutches of eggs, the remaining three sides of the structure and its pitched roof densely applied with sprigging including putti engaged in various pursuits, riding chariots or seated on a lion, cupid on an altar, the corpulent figure of Toby Philpot, Admiral Lord Nelson possibly accompanied by Emma Hamilton, another military figure probably the Duke of Wellington, Hamlet holding poor Yorick's skull, among further sprigged details and trees, 10 in. (26cm) high

Provenance
Christie's London, 3 June 1994, lot 32

A closely related dovecote bearing the incised initials and date 'M.S 1824' was sold by Christie's on 21 January 2003, lot 15. It is illustrated and discussed at length by Millie Manheim who describes it as 'the gem of the Hope McCormick Collection', see Manheim, 1980, pp.96-100. The author suggests that the 'M.S' is in reference to Martha Sherratt, the wife of the potter Obadiah Sherratt. See also Myrna Schkolne, People, Passions, Pastimes and Pleasures, 2006, p.260, where the dated dovecote is illustrated.

The applied relief decoration to the Hope McCormick dovecote is more formal and pertains to symbols of love and affection, with embracing putti and Eros and Anteros tussling under a classical urn. In contrast the present lot has a chaotic fusion of different themes and images, which appear to be chosen at random. The overall effect, highlighted in bright enamel colors is charming and something of which Bennett and Judie Weinstock were particularly fond. Some of the applied scenes including 'The Meet', a hunting scene repeated twice on the dovecote, and the scene of the drunken gentleman resting his head on a barrel, known as 'Grooms Carousing', are depicted on Prattware jugs illustrated by John and Griselda Lewis, Pratt Ware, 1984, p.182 and 196.

Of bullet shape with a crabstock spout, finial and handle, from which tendrils extend in relief around the body, the light sprigging of fruiting vines including two small rats or squirrels, enameled in a distinctive palette of green, turquoise and brown on a puce ground, a stylized butterfly in blue and yellow, 4 1/2 in. Provenance
A. C. J. Wall Collection
Christie's London, 6 June 1988, lot 9

Of generous size with a crabstock handle and rococo scroll molded spout picked out in bright colors, finely enameled on one side with a bucolic piper seated on a mound and admired by a lady, the reverse with two 'Fancy Birds' on a branch, the scenes flanked by detailed sprays of flowers in famille rose enamels, the neck rim and cover with matching elaborate borders, 6 1/2 in. description_block:
A Staffordshire Salt-glazed Stoneware 'Jacobite' Teapot and Cover, Circa 1750
Finely molded as a squat quatrefoil vessel raised on lion mask and paw feet, the crisp pecten shell molding including trailing oak branches and acorns, enameled with leafy branches of mixed flowers and blossoms, each side concealing a leaping figure of a Scotsman brandishing a sword, 5 in. (12.8cm) high

A number of related teapots and small mugs survive in Staffordshire saltglaze with enameled decoration of figures in Highland dress. These are probably from the same workshop as the curious small teapot, lot 16 in this sale, and this distinctive style of enameling is also found on Chinese porcelain enameled in England. While this workshop may have London connections, it might also be evidence of the strong Jacobite sentiments felt in Staffordshire at the time, which is expressed in other decoration on Staffordshire pottery and enamels.

A very similar pecten teapot, with almost identical figure painting, is illustrated by Griselda Lewis, English Pottery, 1956, p.111, fig.109. Another closely related teapot in the Burnap Collection at the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art is illustrated by Ross E Taggart, 1967, no.246, the highland figure described as Bonnie Prince Charlie.

(15.7cm) high

Provenance
With Jonathan Horne

Depictions of Prince Charles Edward Stuart in tartan dress on ceramics and glass in the mid-18th century were derived from several different sources. It was once thought that any portrait in which he is wearing court dress must date prior to the Battle of Culloden, whereas any in tartan must date to after the battle. However, at least two portraits exist of him wearing tartan as a young man and as a young boy, see Geoffrey B Seddon, The Jacobites and their Drinking Glasses, 1995, pp.124-5. On this teapot he is depicted wearing his famous blue velvet bonnet with its white cockade, blue sash and breast star of the Order of the Garter.

A Staffordshire Salt-glazed Stoneware 'Littler's Blue' Teapot and Cover, Circa 1760
Plain globular with a crabstock handle and spout and a pointed mushroom finial, glazed entirely in deep cobalt blue and enameled in white with formal flower sprays, scattered sprigs and florets, 4 1/2 in. (11.5cm) high

Provenance
David Zeitlin Collection

Literature
Arnold Mountford, Staffordshire Salt-glazed Stoneware, 1971, pl.174

The rich blue glaze seen on Staffordshire saltglaze has long been known as 'Littler's Blue'. This is said to have been made by William Littler working in partnership with his brother-in-law Aaron Wedgwood. Littler was mostly interested in making porcelain, initially at Longton Hall and later at West Pans in Scotland, and it seems most likely that Aaron Wedgwood was responsible for the contemporary saltglaze manufacture. Both Jonah Malkin and Thomas and John Wedgwood bought 'Flowered blue ware' from Aaron Wedgwood between 1759 and 1763. 

Raised white enamel decoration is found on some blue-glazed porcelain made by Littler at West Pans at one time thought to have been done by Littler's wife, who accompanied him to Scotland. 

A blue glazed saltglaze coffee pot with floral decoration by the same hand is in the Victoria and Albert Museum, illustrated by Bernard Rackham, Early Staffordshire Pottery, 1951, pl.76. A similar teapot in the Luxmoore Collection is illustrated by Charles F. C. Luxmoore, English Saltglazed Earthenware, 1924, pl.38. This was sold by Sotheby's New York, 15-18 January 2004, lot 196. A puzzle jug seemingly by the same hand is illustrated by Rosalie Wise Sharp, China to Light Up a House, 2016, p.11, fig.E15.

sale_title: The Bennett & Judie Weinstock Collection: Part I
description_block:
Daniel Quigley (Irish, circa 1750-circa 1778)
The chaise match run by the Earls of March and Eglington, Newmarket Heath, 29 August 1750 
signed 'Quigley' (lower right) and extensively inscribed
oil on canvas
99.9 x 212.7 cm (39 1/4 x 83 3/4 in).
framed 114.3 x 227.9cm (45 x 89 3/4 in).

Provenance
Sale, Christie's, London, 22 April 1983, lot 21 (as Property of a gentleman)

Literature
A. Crookshank and The Knight of Glin, The Painter of Ireland, c.1660-1920, London, 1978, p. 64

The Chaise Match Run is derived from James Seymour's most celebrated composition, the prime version of which is now in the Yale Center for British Art (inv. no. B2014.5.25). Other versions by Daniel Quigley were previously in the Hamilton Palace Collection and another larger work, 145 x 253 cm, in a private collection (see: S. Deuchar, Sporting Art in Eighteenth Century England: A Social and Political History, New Haven, 1988, ill., fig. 12).

The subject enjoyed great popularity, as attested to by the number of copies known, such as that by Thomas Butler (offered Sotheby's, New York, 16 April, 1998, lot 28). A subsequent engraving by Bodger further ensured the popularity of the subject.

The present lot depicts an event undertaken as the result of a wager by the 3rd Earl of March and the 10th Earl of Eglington against Theobald Taaffe and Andrew Sproule. The run took place on Newmarket Heath of 29 August, 1750. Lord March wagered 1,000 guineas that he could run a four-wheeled carriage nineteen miles in less than an hour with four horses and one postilion. In carriages specifically designed for the occasion by Wright of Long Acre, both earls managed to win their bet with Lord March completing the course in just 53 minutes and 27 seconds.

Aside from his omission of the crowds, Quigley depicted the subject with great accuracy, even including the groom in red riding ahead of the carriages to clear the course. The present work is one of the larger repetitions of the subject and is about 30cm. wider than Seymour's version but is much more panoramic in format and includes the detailed explanation of the race itself.

Daniel Quigley is currently the only recorded Irish sporting artist of the mid-18th century (see M.A. Wingfield, A Dictionary of Sporting Artists 1650-1990, Woodbridge, Suffolk, 1992, p.231). His Godolphin Arabian was offered in the sale of the Contents of Glyn Cywarch, The Property of Lord Harlech, Bonhams, London, 29 March 2017, lot 99.

An Important Staffordshire Lead-glazed Creamware Dovecote of Whieldon-type, Circa 1755-60
Modeled as an octagonal two-storey building, doves emerging from the pierced windows and resting on ledges, further doves perched on the tiled roof above, the doorway molded in relief with a man and child standing beneath the title 'A NEW PAVILION', raised on a knopped stem and domed foot, 8 1/2 in. (22cm) high

Provenance
With D M & P Manheim

This form appears to be derived from a saltglaze stoneware prototype. See the teapot in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, object no.45.12.44a,b, which is of the same architectural, octagonal form, with New Pavilion noted above the doorway. However, the many windows are all 'closed', making it viable as a vessel for holding tea. The earthenware reinvention as a dovecote elevates the basic functional form to an ornamental object; the pierced windows and the addition of the doves give the Georgian house form a playful aesthetic, not least because of the discrepancy in scale between the human figures in the doorway and the oversized birds.

An almost identical example was bequeathed to the British Museum in 1891 by G R Harding, accession no.1891,0524.3. Another example is said to have been destroyed in the infamous Alexandra Palace Fire of 1873. More recently, a similar dovecote was sold by Brunk on 22 October 2025, lot 716. See also the pair of dovecotes in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, object no.40.171.7&8.

description_block:
A Staffordshire Lead-glazed 'Landskip' Teapot and Cover of Whieldon-type, Circa 1765
Globular with a lobed body crisply molded in relief with landscape panels including cattle, sheep and swimming swans, the panels framed with rococo diaper and basketwork, striped in grey and green underglaze oxides, the scroll handle and curved spout also with basket molding glazed in brown, the cover with a sheep forming the finial, 4 1/2 in. (12.3cm) high

On 11 January 1764, William Greatbatch invoiced Wedgwood for a series of models including the modelling of a 'Landskip Tpt'. It has therefore been assumed that Greatbatch modelled all such landscape teapots, but this may not have been the case. Two block molds were discovered at the Wedgwood factory corresponding to this type of teapot, and these are illustrated by David Barker, William Greatbatch, 1990, pl.9. It is significant, however, that no shards of 'Landskip' pattern were found on the Greatbatch site and instead these have been discovered elsewhere in Staffordshire including on the site of Thomas Whieldon's factory at Fenton Vivian. A similar example in the Victoria and Albert Museum, accession no.C.21&A-1940, is illustrated by Donald Towner, Creamware, 1978, pl.8B. Another was sold by Sotheby's New York on 9 December 1986, lot 66.

A Staffordshire Lead-glazed Teapot and Cover of Whieldon-type, Circa 1765-70
Of hexagonal form, a 'Melon-ware' glaze of alternate green and yellow stripes, modeled in low relief with panels of flowering plants on a ground of a fine repeating geometric pattern, the scroll handle and spout with basketwork molding glazed in green, 4 1/2 in. (12.4cm) high

This teapot belongs to a class of early Staffordshire teawares with relief decoration on a ground of geometric or diaper ornament. Mostly Chinoiserie, these pieces were produced in unglazed redware and in cream-colored earthenware with a variety of glaze types. Many of the designs were based on images in George Edwards and Matthew Darley's 'A New Book of Chinese Designs' published in 1754. This teapot is a particularly rare model.

A rare Staffordshire Lead-glazed Double-walled Teapot and Cover of Whieldon-type, Circa 1765
Of curious cinquefoil shape with a bifurcated twig handle and leaf-molded spout, the body double-walled, the outer layer molded and pierced with panels of flowering prunus plants, the cover similarly modelled and pierced, glazed overall in bright green, 5 1/2 in. (14.5cm) high

See the example in the Henry Weldon Collection illustrated and discussed by Peter Williams and Pat Halfpenny, A Passion for Pottery, 2000, pp.168-9.

For the same model in unglazed redware see Henry Sandon, Coffee Pots and Teapots, 1973, pl.17.

sale_title: The Bennett & Judie Weinstock Collection: Part I
description_block:
'Norah's Teapot': A Celebrated Whieldon-type Punch Pot and Cover, Circa 1765-70
Of most generous size, the globular body finely turned with all-over horizontal bands, the scroll handle with an inviting thumbrest, the snake-headed spout with delicate floral scroll molding, decorated under the clear lead glaze with vertical stripes of grey, brown, green and ochre yellow, 9 in. (23cm) high

Provenance
Mrs Norah Ambrose, Merseyside
Sotheby's London, 18 October 1988, lot 548
With Alistair Sampson Antiques

In 1988 this punch pot featured on the BBC Antiques Roadshow. Viewers worldwide shared a moment of discovery when Mrs Ambrose opened the large box which she had struggled to push along a very long queue. Ceramics expert David Battie revealed her giant teapot wrapped in a towel whilst Norah explained that her family had used the pot for making tea for generations, but it was really too big and in recent years it had resided in the box on top of a wardrobe. David Battie explained that it was actually more likely a punch pot and was more than two hundred years old, a rare survivor from early Staffordshire. Norah's shock at hearing the valuation- more than £5000- became one of the magic moments of the popular television series. Following the programme, Mrs Ambrose sold the punch pot at Sotheby's where it made £14,300. As was extensively reported in the media, in 1988 the proceeds of the sale were sufficient to enable Norah to buy her council-house. Norah Ambrose became something of a celebrity and in her final years she attended many recording days with the Antiques Roadshow. Meanwhile, Norah's Teapot has become a small part of British television history.

The Weinstocks were struck by the pot's qualities when Alistair Sampson exhibited it after its sale at Sotheby's. The massive scale of this punch pot, and its precise turned decoration gives emphasis to the rich underglaze coloring. Bennett and Judie were also keenly aware of the charming story of its discovery and kept a newspaper cutting inside to make sure it was not forgotten.

description_block:
A Staffordshire Lead-glazed Apple Teapot and Cover of Whieldon-type, Circa 1760-65
Naturalistically modeled in the shape of a single apple, sprigged in relief with green and ochre leaves against a running tortoiseshell glaze, the pot and the cover also applied with matching rope-like stems, the crabstock handle, spout and finial each glazed in green, 4 1/2 in. (12cm) high

Provenance
With Ginsburg & Levy of Madison Avenue

In the catalogue of the Henry Weldon Collection, English Pottery 1650-1800, 1990, p.177, no.83, Leslie Grigsby illustrates a related teapot together with an unglazed kiln waster of a similar cover excavated in Town Road, Hanley. William Greatbatch wrote to Josiah Wedgwood, circa 1762 '... please send word by the bearer whether we should or not have sent you an apple teapot and if you would have leaves on the side same as used to be...' The leaves on this teapot are very individual with curious rope-twist stalks, placed so that they continue onto the cover. Another apple teapot in the Mint Museum is of the same basic form although more squat in proportion, see Brian Gallagher, British Ceramics, 2015, p.71, cat. no. 32.4.

description_block:
An Exceptional Staffordshire Solid Agate Squirrel Teapot and Cover, Circa 1750-55
The animal on its haunches and clutching a nut in its paws, the head forming the cover, with a slender spout, the handle notched, press-molded from clay marbled in cream and chestnut-brown below a clear lead glaze, 6 in. (15.8cm) high

Provenance
Rev C J Sharp Collection
Sotheby's, 25 November 1997, lot 191

Literature
Frank Tilley, Teapots and Tea, 1957, pl.III, no.13

A skilful potter created this squirrel teapot by pressing into a mold thin slabs of marbled clay, neatly folded to produce a pattern that has been compared to an elephant's tooth when polished. Diana Edwards notes the rarity of squirrel teapots in solid agate earthenware, illustrating an example from Temple Newsam House alongside a white saltglaze version. See 'The influence of Salt-Glazed Stoneware on Creamware', in Creamware and Pearlware Re-Examined, 2007, p.150, figs. 7 and 8. See lot 30 for a square form solid agate teapot also with 'elephant tooth' decoration.

A hand-written paper label on the base suggests that this may have once been in the Shand Kydd Collection, to which Frank Tilley supplied many pieces.

description_block:
A Staffordshire Solid Agate Chocolate Pot and Cover, Circa 1740-50
Of gently spreading hexagonal shape, applied with a looped strap side handle at right angles to the serpentine spout which is very crisply molded with pecten shells, the domed cover with a 'Dog of Fo' finial, finely marbled overall in brown, grey-blue and cream 'solid agate' clay, 8 1/2 in. (22.8cm) high

This delicate chocolate pot was press-molded from thin sheets of marbled clay, a remarkable achievement by unknown potters in Staffordshire during the reign of George II. The shape, sometimes referred to as "lighthouse form", probably derives from English silver chocolate and coffee pots of the early 18th century. A glazed redware chocolate pot of similar proportions with agateware panels is illustrated by Rosalie Wise Sharp, Ceramics, Ethics & Scandal, 2002, p.40. Another example in glazed redware was sold by Bonhams 8 September 2004, lot 60.

A Rare Staffordshire Salt-glazed Stoneware Teapot and Cover, Circa 1750-60
Of hexagonal form, molded with six chinoiserie landscape panels, one with a Chinese gentleman holding a pennant or fishing rod, painted in bright enamels on a vibrant yellow ground, the cover surmounted with a recumbent animal, possibly a lion, 5 1/2 in. (14.3c) high

sale_title: The Bennett & Judie Weinstock Collection: Part I
description_block:
Miss Bignells: An Important Creamware Coffee Pot and Cover, Circa 1770
Of large size and plain baluster shape with a spreading foot and milled rims, the double rope-twist handle with floret and leaf terminals, scrolling leaves at the base of the spout, painted in black, red, green and yellow with three fine ladies standing in a garden, one gesturing to a birdcage and to the bird in its open door, the other ladies holding a nosegay and a singing bird, titled in black above 'MISS BIGNELLS', the reverse with a grand three-storey house with outbuildings and domestic fowl running free in the front, the cover with a flower spray and a floret finial, 10 in. (26.4cm) high

Provenance
Phillips, 11 June 1986, lot 143, and illustrated on the catalogue cover

The decoration on this coffee pot has hidden meanings, suggesting coffee may not have been the only beverage that was served by the fine ladies at Miss Bignell's establishment. 

The birdcage was a popular symbol of Marriage and it also represented Liberty or freedom from marriage. A birdcage could be a symbol of a woman's chastity, which was intact if the bird was still in the cage, but if the door was open, then the bird had flown. A birdcage therefore represented the social, domestic, and legal constraints of marriage. However a bird released from confinement embodied Liberty, the carefree, lack of constraints and freedom of the single life. 

One of the fine ladies places her hand on the open birdcage, perhaps read by the 18th century viewer as an act of invitation. Another lady holds a released bird, able to fly free. On the reverse of the coffee pot, many different birds have gathered in front of the house, without any barriers or constraints.

sale_title: The Bennett & Judie Weinstock Collection: Part I
description_block:
Two Large Staffordshire Pearlware Royal Busts, Circa 1820
Probably depicting Prince Leopold and Princess Charlotte, a garter star and epaulets on his red jacket, she with a blue sash worn across her red dress below gilt jewels, her hair piled up in ringlets below a tiara studded with roses and plumes, the plinth bases picked out in bright colors simulating marbled hardstone, 19 in. (49cm) and 20 in. (51cm) high

Provenance
With Jonathan Horne

These impressive, almost life-sized busts have been assigned various identities over the years. A similar bust of a gentleman, presumed to be King George IV from the Rous Lench Collection was sold by Christie's, 29 May 1990, lot 139. However, an undecorated example in the Henry Willett Collection incised 'D.L Sept. 9th 1832', suggests that it shows King William IV, see Stella Beddoe, A Potted History, 2015, p.26, fig.072. On close inspection, the male bust in this lot has a thinner, longer face, and his fashionable grips are worn much shorter. We might then conclude that this depicts another figure entirely. 

Jonathan Horne believed that he represented the dashing figure of Prince Leopold of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld, who was married to Princess Charlotte, the only daughter of King George IV. Their short marriage ended when Charlotte tragically died in childbirth in 1817. The identity of the female bust could therefore be Charlotte, who was extremely popular with the public and commemorated before and after her untimely death. A bust of Charlotte on a different base is illustrated by Beddoe, 2015, p.23, fig.069.

A female bust left in the white from the Mario Buatta Collection is similar to the present lot but has a more elaborate tiara and varied hairstyle. It was sold by Sotheby's on 25 January 2020, lot 803 and was identified as Queen Caroline, Princess Charlotte's mother.

sale_title: The Bennett & Judie Weinstock Collection: Part I
description_block:
Polito's Menagerie: An Extraordinary Staffordshire Table Base Group, Circa 1820
Attributed to the 'Sherratt' pot bank, the handsome six-panelled door amply lit by three lanterns, surmounted by a brightly colored banner unfolded to reveal an elephant with a crenelated howdah, surrounded by exotic animals including a lion and a tiger, birds and monkeys perched above the inscription 'POLITOS ROYAL MENAGERIE OF THE WONDERFULL BURDS AND BEASTS FROM MOST PARTS OF THE WORLD: LION & C.', thirteen figures and two monkeys populating the base and steps below, including a man playing a barrel organ, one monkey atop a second barrel organ, which is played by a figure simultaneously blowing a bugle horn, the jolly doorkeeper with her hands in a muff, two trumpeters and a drummer standing by a tall, elegantly dressed lady, six patrons exiting the show including a young child at her mother's hip on the bottom step, all raised on a rectangular table base with six sturdy claw feet, ht. 13, lg. 12 in.

Although the obsession with exotic animals had long existed in England, an appetite catered to by permanent menageries, it was not until the late 18th and early 19th centuries that travelling menageries evolved to become precursors of the modern zoo. Myrna Schkolne has researched and written extensively on the history of travelling menageries and their representation in Staffordshire pottery, see Travelling Menageries 1700-1850, 2024. 

Rivalled perhaps only by Wombwell's menagerie, Stephen Polito's travelling caravan of wondrous creatures became the most famous of its kind in the early 19th century. The Italian-born Polito toured showgrounds and town squares in England and Ireland and patrons paid to enter the grand façade and tour the caravans containing the variety of beasts held within, which included a "striped Bengal tyger". In July 1808, The Staffordshire Advertiser reported that Polito's menagerie had come to Wolverhampton, not far from the Staffordshire Potteries and it was perhaps this tour that initially inspired potters like Obadiah Sherratt to create the remarkable earthenware models.

There is great variety in the extant models of Polito's and Wombwell's menageries, but the most imposing are the examples on wide table bases, with separately modeled steps leading up to the entrance. An example of this type is in the Glaisher bequest, Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge, accession no.C.965-1928. A slightly more compact, yet still hugely impressive version was sold by Bonhams on 14 December 2023, lot 245, where there are just five figures nestled in front of the doorway to the attraction. The larger Polito's menageries nearly always feature an open door, perhaps to allow for better ventilation during firing for such a heavy and elaborate model. The wide range of enamel colors would have necessitated many firings, each increasing the risk of failure in the kiln and at extra cost.

The present lot is perhaps unrivalled in the complexity and fullness of its modeling, with so many figures enlivening the table base and steps. A slightly later Wombwell's Menagerie from the Herbert and Nancy Hunt Collection comes close in terms of scale and presence, see Myrna Schkolne, Holding the Past, 2014, p.89.

Although Stephen Polito and his wife Sarah both died in 1814, the menagerie continued under the auspices of Stephen's brother, John, who reportedly purchased it at "enormous expense". As the decade came to a close, Wombwell's rising dominance spelled out the decline of Polito's once grand reputation and in 1823 Polito's went to Europe and never returned to Britain's shores. The long held belief that the menagerie sank during a storm at sea in 1835 is now thought to be apocryphal. 

Remaining as testament to the these popular menageries and the imagination and ambition of the potters who sought to reproduce them, the large Polito's menagerie must count as one of the most appealing and important of all Staffordshire models.

A Large Pearlware Group of a Cow and Calf, Circa 1820-40
Probably Scottish, the young calf nursing, both animals sponged with black markings, the rectangular stepped base with canted corners and with unusual geometric sponged decoration in blue, green, puce and black, 7 in. (19cm) high, 11 in. (29cm) long

Provenance
Hope McCormick Collection
Christie's, 21 January 2003, lot 35

Literature
Illustrated in Millie Manheim, Selections from the Hope McCormick Collection of Staffordshire Pottery, 1980, pl.14, pp.42-43

In her catalogue of the McCormick Collection, Millie Manheim suggests this extraordinary group could be attributed to Portobello. The underglaze coloring, especially the use of black, puce and blue, is indeed a strong indication of a Scottish origin. The markings suggest that these are Friesian cattle. The sensitive modeling and generous scale of the group gives it character and great presence.

sale_title: The Bennett & Judie Weinstock Collection: Part I
description_block:
A Very Large Pearlware Cow Creamer and Cover, Circa 1800-20
Staffordshire or Yorkshire and probably a shop display model, the sizable beast standing on a rectangular base washed in underglaze blue, the cow splashed with irregular patches of brown and ochre, 9 1/2 in. (25cm) high, 12 1/2 (32cm) long

Many oversized models are believed to have been intended for display in shop windows, in this case not to advertise ceramics for sale but instead this would have promoted the sale of fresh milk. Indeed, later in the 19th century large cow models from Staffordshire were occasionally titled 'Milk Sold Here'. Earlier cow creamers in this larger scale are very rarely encountered.

An Impressive Yorkshire Pearlware Jug, Dated 1792
Molded beneath the spout in high relief with a large ewe and lamb recumbent on a grassy mound, inscribed below 'W T, 1792' painted in Pratt type colors with formal floral sprays below a formal border, 11 in. (28.2cm) high

Provenance
Sotheby's, 4 June 1996, lot 142
With Alistair Sampson Antiques

The probable attribution to the Swinton Pottery in Yorkshire is based on comparison with a small number of wares painted with identical borders and flowers. See John D Griffin, The Yorkshire Potteries, 2012, pp.94-96, where a teapot also dated 1792 is inscribed for a 'Mary Bealby' of 'Newton' in West Riding. No similar sheep jug would appear to be recorded. The three-dimensionality of the ewe and lamb is strikingly effective and has been achieved by adapting the mold of a free-standing model of a sheep, which would have sat on a hollow base.

A Leeds Pearlware Model of a Horse, Circa 1820-30
The piebald stallion with sponged black coat and ochre chequered saddle cloth, standing on a shaped rectangular base densely sponged in green, ochre and black, 17 in. (44cm) high, 13 1/2 in. (34.5cm) long

The base on which this horse stands provides better support for the weight of the animal, compared with the lower, thinner bases which often required integral supports to the underside. The color palette used suggests a date around 1820-30. Although referred to as Leeds horses, it is possible that other potteries, especially in the north east of England or perhaps Scotland used the same molds to produce similar models. See the footnote to lot 57 where the link with Leeds Pottery is traced back to potters in the 19th century.

description_block:
A Pair of Creamware Wall Pockets Based on Theatrical Figures, Circa 1775-80
Figures traditionally known as Hamlet and Ophelia have been adapted to form winged caryatids, open at the back and pierced for wall hanging, the figures of an actor and actress flanked by leaf-like wings and applied with florets picked out with brown and dark ochre underglaze washes, he 13 1/2 in. (34cm) high, she 12 1/2 in. (31cm) high

Provenance
With Wynn A. Sayman

This extraordinary pair is clearly based on the creamware figures traditionally known as Hamlet and Ophelia. For a large pair of similar date in the Harold Mackintosh collection see Early English Figure Pottery, 1938, p.43, nos.83 and 98. Another pair was sold by Bonhams, December 15 1993, lot 13. The central portion of these pockets have been cast from the original creamware molds, with additions including the wings and flowers, creating a unique pair of folk-art ornaments. It is tempting to suggest that these are provincial productions, from a pottery such as Bovey Tracey. It is also worth comparing these with a sphinx candlestick in the Henry Weldon Collection, Catalogue 1990, pp.454-5, no.289.

sale_title: The Bennett & Judie Weinstock Collection: Part I
description_block:
A Documentary Creamware Teapot and Cover, Dated 1772
Sponged and painted with manganese and green oxides, the inscription incised and picked out in blue, 'Capt Willm Beale in the Bridgwater Casell 1772', the entwined handle with foliate terminals, leaf-molded spout also washed in green, 6 1/2 in. (16cm) high

The 'scratch blue' manner of the inscription is reminiscent of some Bovey Tracey earthenware and stoneware made in nearby Devon. However, a Staffordshire or Yorkshire origin is also possible.

William Beale was born in 1739 into a family heavily involved in maritime trade and merchant activities in Bridgwater, Somerset. During the 1770s William's name frequently appears in the borough's commercial court records, although he is not listed with the title of Captain. Bridgwater Castle had been virtually destroyed by Parliamentary forces during the English civil wars in the 1640s but by the 1770s the site had been redeveloped. The area surrounding the old castle ruins (such as Castle Street) became a hub for business and Georgian housing.

Probably Yorkshire, of baluster shape, the neck neatly turned with horizontal bands, the lower body with vertical flutes, with fine molded gadrooning at the neck rim and with a milled footrim, applied with an elaborate entwined stalk handle with leaf sprig terminals, and a serpentine spiral-ribbed spout, the cover with a large flower finial, sponged in manganese and splashed in green, 11 in. Provenance
Sotheby's New York, 9 December 1986, lot 73

A Yorkshire origin is based on a number of features associated with the Rothwell pottery, near Leeds. These include the yellowish-cream ground, and the emerald green oxide splashes. The molded oval-bead and diagonal-dash border appear on a creamware jug attributed to Rothwell, see Donald Towner, Creamware, 1978, p.163, pl.87. 

Of impressive proportions, this may have been intended to serve punch rather than coffee.

description_block:
A Fine Staffordshire Lead-glazed Chocolate Pot and Cover of Whieldon-type, Circa 1760-65
Of conical form with a crabstock handle at right angles to the S-shaped spout, crisply sprigged in relief with vines, leaves and tendrils, splashed with underglaze green and brown oxide decoration which continues inside the vessel, 8 1/2 in. (22.8cm) high

Provenance
Mr and Mrs Frank Freeth Collection
Kanter Collection
With Jonathan Horne

Literature
Old English Pottery Collected and Catalogued by Mr and Mrs Frank Freeth, 1896, p.27, pl.11, no.1

This is a particularly good example of 'Tortoiseshell Ware', a term favoured by potters in the 18th century for productions decorated with metallic oxides applied before glazing. Thomas Whieldon used the term as early as 1749, and this class of ware has become known as 'Whieldon' or 'Whieldon-type', even though many other manufacturers produced identical glazes. Another chocolate pot with a darker brown tortoiseshell glaze was sold by Bonhams 13 November 2013, Lot 117

sale_title: The Bennett & Judie Weinstock Collection: Part I
description_block:
An Exceptional Lead-Glazed Creamware Teapot and Cover Attributed to Enoch Booth of Tunstall, Circa 1743-50
The small, flattened body supported on three mask and paw feet, applied with a distinctive biting-snake or lamprey handle, plain spout and 'Dog-of-Fo' finial, the cream-colored body painted underglaze in manganese and green with a curious cartoon-like figure holding trailing flowers, the same figure repeated in reverse on the other side, 4 in. (10.5cm) high

Extensive research by Pat Halfpenny and others has traced the family and career of Enoch Booth, who was apprenticed in 1717 to Thomas Heath of Shelton. Married in 1728 to Ann Child, the Booths inherited land in Tunstall, Staffordshire where Enoch built a potworks. According to the early chronicler Simeon Shaw, Enoch Booth developed the earliest cream-colored earthenware. Key pieces of creamware linked to Booth include a creamware punchbowl in the British Museum initialled 'EB 1743', and a teapot in the Henry Weldon Collection inscribed 'F.Morgan Tunstall Oct 20th 1743'. A significant teapot in the Potteries Museum uses the same handle as the present lot, and also a similar Dog of Fo, both as the finial and inverted as feet. See Williams and Halfpenny, A Passion for Pottery, 2000, pp.164-166.

sale_title: The Bennett & Judie Weinstock Collection: Part I
description_block:
A Staffordshire Lead-glazed Creamware Royal Commemorative Teapot and Cover, Circa 1785
Modeled as the head of King George III, inscribed around the rim 'GOD SAVE THE KING', the reverse molded with the head of Queen Charlotte, titled around the rim 'AND GOD SAVE THE QE...', lightly colored with underglaze oxides, a scroll handle and fluted spout applied on either side, the neck and domed cover also molded with shell-like flutes, 6 1/2 in. (17.5cm) high

Provenance
With Wynn A Sayman

The portrait of the King strongly resembles those used for cups and jugs commemorating Admiral Lord Rodney. The same mold was used or subtly adapted by the potters, allowing the inscription to confirm the identity of the Royal couple. A two-sided loving cup in the Maritime Museum, Greenwich, collection no.AAA4374. depicts two identical male portraits titled in similar impressed letters 'SUCCESS TO LORD RODNEY', 'AND GOD SAVE THE KING'.

sale_title: The Bennett & Judie Weinstock Collection: Part I
description_block:
An Interesting Staffordshire Lead-glazed Creamware Cradle, Circa 1785
Attributed to Ralph Wood, modeled as a rectangular canopied crib on simple rockers, every part of the exterior and interior 'sprigged' with relief ornament, mostly neo-classical in style including urns, patterae, festoons and various florets, along with several figures of a gardener, portrait medallions of a Bacchic maiden, a titled portrait medallion of 'Admiral Rodney' and a incomplete medallion of a ship titled 'Ville de....', in the base of the interior a child lies beneath a mat of flowerheads, 9 in. (23.5cm) long, 5 1/2 in. (14.5cm) high

Provenance
With Tilley & Co, Symons Street, London
Sir Harold Mackintosh Collection
Christie's, 2 June 1986, lot 42

Literature
Sir Harold Mackintosh, Early English Figure Pottery, 1938, p.93, no.135

In his catalogue, Lord Mackintosh recorded the traditional story, passed on to him by Frank Tilley, that the cradle was made to commemorate the death of Lord Rodney's infant daughter who died soon after Rodney's victories over the French in 1782. At the Battle of the Saintes on April 12, 1782, Admiral Rodney had defeated the French fleet and captured their magnificent flagship, the Ville de Paris. Tilley believed that the young girl bedecked with flowers represented Lord Rodney's child, and that the cradle filled with flowers was intended to preserve her memory. No other example would appear to be recorded.

sale_title: The Bennett & Judie Weinstock Collection: Part I
description_block:
An Important Staffordshire Creamware 'Shenstone and Fair Hebe' Teapot and Cover by Jean Voyez, Circa 1770-80
Celebrating the poet William Shenstone and his best-known composition, modeled as a rustic tree stump encircled by figures, one side with a scene from the ballad showing two seated figures, a scroll behind titled 'Fair Hebe', the reverse with putti supporting a titled portrait of the poet, a partly-concealed signature 'I VOYEZ' near the base, in lead-glazed earthenware with Whieldon-type underglaze coloring of green, blue and cream on a brown background simulating bark, applied with a crabstock handle and spout, the cover with a leafy stalk forming the finial, 5 1/2 (15cm) high

An identical example with a matching stand is in the Delhom Collection in the Mint Museum and this is discussed at length in the Delhom Gallery Guide to English Pottery, no. 1, 1982. One of Mellanay Delhom's favourite pieces, she researched a detailed paper, following on from Robert Charleston's ECC paper on Jean Voyez, Vol 5, Pt.1, 1960. The notorious modeller Jean Voyez provided molds to several Staffordshire manufacturers, and while the maker of this extraordinary teapot remains elusive, its significance echoes its great rarity. One other very similar teapot, also signed I Voyez, is in the Burnap Collection at the Nelson-Atkins Gallery of Art, Catalogue, revised 1967, p.142, no.545.

sale_title: The Bennett & Judie Weinstock Collection: Part I
description_block:
An Extremely Large Wedgwood Creamware Coffee Pot or Punch Pot and Cover, Dated 1785
Made for the Dutch market, one side printed in outline and hand-colored with a ship incorporating the inscription 'DE AGNES EN DE YOANNA VAN OSTENDE 1785', the name 'NICOLACS CANOEN' painted above, the other side painted with a family, a husband and wife with their daughter perhaps, taking a walk in the grounds of a large house, 13 1/2 in. (34.5cm) high, impressed WEDGWOOD

Provenance
With Alistair Sampson Antiques

This sizable coffee pot, or perhaps a punch pot, refers to the maritime trade from Ostend. The sailing ship depicted, 'Agnes and Yoanna of Ostend', was named after its owners, Agnes Verdonck (1743-1835) and Joannes Van den Hove, married in Ostend in 1773. The Imperial Habsburg flag, as depicted on the coffee pot, refers to the administration of the Austrian Netherlands, present-day Belgium. A matching plate also dated 1785 and an oval dish, bearing the names of the ship owners, were sold by Rob Michiels Auctions, Bruges, 25 February 2023, lot 1461. See also Robin Reilly, Wedgwood Vol.I, 1989, p.305, fig.374 for another large coffee pot inscribed for 'Johannes Verdonk en Johanna Verdonk'.

Provenance
With Taylor Williams Antiques, Chicago (spaniel box)
Lawrence Gould Collection (musical instruments box)

Literature
Susan Benjamin, English Enamel Boxes, 1978, p.82 (musical instruments box)

The transfer-print of putti with a lion and military trophies occurs on earlier London enamel boxes, the design attributed to Ravenet, see Egan Mew, Battersea Enamels, 1926, fig.23. Although recumbent spaniels were a popular motif on South Staffordshire boxes, the example in the present lot is particularly finely modeled and painted and by repute comes from the celebrated Ionides Collection.

The writing box of rectangular form with a serpentine front, painted with a portrait of a fine lady, smaller floral panels reserved on a deep blue ground with white diaper and gilt scrolls, the gilt metal interior including enamel-topped ink and pounce pots, 6.4cm wide, the nÃ©cessaire with rural scenes and flowers on a pale blue ground, the fitments including a pair of scissors and a spoon, 3 in. (7.3cm) high

A travel writing box of this form is illustrated by Therle and Bernard Hughes, English Painted Enamels, 1967, p.71, fig.36. A similar nécessaire painted on a green ground was sold by Bonhams on 11 June 2025, lot 174. A blue-ground example from the Nellie Ionides Collection was sold by Sotheby's on 24 May 1976, lot 16. Both objects would have been fashionable and useful items for the 18th century lady or gentleman to carry on their person.
